P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Ireland applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and payments between EU countries, as well as between EU and non-EU countries.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Ireland-specific source on account rules was captured.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Sole traders must register with Revenue within 30 days of starting to trade, using Form TR1 via the Revenue Online Service (ROS). A business name other than your own is registered with the CRO. Returns (Form 11) are due by 31 October, or mid-November via ROS. Your PPS number serves as your tax reference.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: The Personal Public Service (PPS) number is used as the tax reference for individuals, including sole traders. Official TIN description (OECD sheet): "Natural Persons: Ireland issues TINs, which are not reported on official documents of identification. The number used to identify taxpayers is the Personal Public Service Number (PPS No). This number is issued by the Department of Social Protection but is also used by the Revenue Commissioners to identify taxpayers. PPS-numbers are issued automatically on birth registration for children born in the country."

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Tax residents of Ireland are taxed on worldwide income (see quoted rules for exceptions such as remittance-basis regimes). 20% and 40% bands (single person: 20% up to EUR 44,000 in 2026), plus USC and PRSI. Inference (general source principle, not quoted): work performed while living in Ireland for foreign clients is normally taxable in Ireland. Confirmed by KPMG: the single person's 20% band is EUR 44,000 in 2026, rising to EUR 46,500 in 2027 (Budget 2027). Self-employed PRSI (Class S) is 4.2%, rising to 4.35% from 1 October 2026, with a minimum of EUR 650 a year. USC for the self-employed in 2026: 0.5% to EUR 12,012, 2% to EUR 28,700, 3% to EUR 70,044, 8% to EUR 100,000, and 11% above EUR 100,000 (the surcharge on self-employment income). Total income up to EUR 13,000 is exempt from USC.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: The standard VAT rate is 23%. Irish registration thresholds are EUR 42,500 (services) and EUR 85,000 (goods) on a rolling 12-month basis. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Ireland VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Ireland VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Ireland, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

sources.quote: These rules apply to both companies and organisations (public and private) in the EU and those based outside the EU who offer goods or services in the EU , such as Facebook or Amazon, whenever these companies request or re-use the personal data of individuals in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
